# IRA and 401(k) rules

Notes from the financial planning class handout.

## IRA contribution limits

You can put up to $7,000 a year into an IRA, or $8,000 if you are 50 or older. The limit covers all your IRAs combined, and you need earned income at least as large as what you contribute. You have until the tax-filing deadline to make the contribution for the prior year.

## 401(k) contribution limits

An employee can defer up to $23,500 a year into a 401(k) from pay, and people 50 or older can add a $7,500 catch-up, for $31,000. These limits are separate from the IRA limit, so you can use both. The employer's match does not count against your own limit.

## Traditional versus Roth

A traditional account gives a tax break now and is taxed when withdrawn. A Roth gets no break now, but qualified withdrawals are tax-free. Roth IRA eligibility phases out at higher incomes, while Roth 401(k) has no income limit.

## Early withdrawals

Taking money out of an IRA or 401(k) before age 59½ usually costs a 10% additional tax on top of ordinary income tax. Exceptions include disability, a first-time home purchase (up to $10,000 from an IRA), and unreimbursed medical costs over 7.5% of income. Contributions to a Roth IRA, but not the earnings, can be taken out at any time without penalty.

## Required minimum distributions

You must start taking money out of traditional accounts at age 73. The yearly amount comes from an IRS table based on your balance and age. Missing it triggers a penalty on the amount you should have taken.

## Employer match in general

Many employers match part of what you put in, which is an immediate return on your contribution. The rate and the schedule differ for each plan: look in your plan documents, and always contribute at least enough to get the whole match.

## Rolling over an old 401(k)

Ask the old plan for a direct rollover to an IRA or your new plan. A check made out to you triggers 20% withholding, and you must make up that amount from other money within 60 days.
